note: Cranial muscles are organised by pharyngeal arch of origin. Arch identity, marked by cranial nerve, is the primary homology criterion here and is far more constraining than in the limb: Abdala & Diogo (2010) note that in the head each rhombomeric neural crest population forms both the connective tissue of specific muscles and their attachment sites, so cranial muscle attachment is identity-bound in a way limb attachment is not.

muscles.name: Adductor mandibulae complex
muscles.developmental: First (mandibular) pharyngeal arch mesoderm; connective tissue from mandibular-stream neural crest.

consensus.origin: Lateral and dorsal surfaces of the palatoquadrate or its ossified derivatives — in amniotes, the temporal region of the skull.
consensus.insertion: Medial, dorsal and lateral surfaces of the lower jaw (Meckel's cartilage or the dentary and adjacent bones).
consensus.action: Adducts (closes) the lower jaw. The principal biting muscle in all gnathostomes.
consensus.innervation: Trigeminal nerve (CN V), mandibular division — invariant across Gnathostomata.

occurrences.note: Lampreys have no jaws. Their feeding musculature (velar and lingual apparatus) is not homologous with the gnathostome adductor complex, though some of it is mandibular-arch derived and trigeminal-innervated.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae
occurrences.note: Relatively undivided, giving the plesiomorphic gnathostome condition.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias, from Huber et al.'s descriptions. From the palatoquadrate onto Meckel's cartilage — the primary jaw adductor in all cartilaginous fishes, with multiple divisions. Both elements are homology groups here: the palatoquadrate is the same record as the amniote quadrate and the mammalian incus, so this row and the mammalian masseter's are visibly on descendants of one bone.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae A1–A3, Aω
occurrences.note: Extensively subdivided in teleosts in correlation with the mobile upper jaw. Jayaram et al. (1983) describe the mandibular and hyoid muscle complexes in three species of the catfish genus Arius and find the myological differences taxonomically informative at species level — a reminder that the subdivision pattern varies below the clade level this dataset records.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae A2 + A2-PVM + pseudotemporalis
occurrences.divisionNote: Ambystoma mexicanum. Three adductors, and the criterion separating two of them is a nerve: the mandibular branch of the trigeminal (CN V3) runs BETWEEN the A2 and the A2-PVM. Worth reading against the pigeon, where Jones et al. find the adductor mandibulae externus lateral to both CN V2 and CN V3 where amniotes usually have it between them — the same nerve, used the same way, giving different answers in two taxa. Ziermann & Diogo note the anterior fibres of the A2-PVM look like part of the pseudotemporalis in both larva and adult.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma mexicanum, adult (neotenic). The A2 arises from the squamosal and inserts dorsally on the dentary. In the LARVA both ends are different: it arises from the palatoquadrate and the orbital cartilage and inserts on Meckel's cartilage, and during development it swings from vertical to diagonal. The A2-PVM's attachments are given for the larva only — palatoquadrate at the commissura quadrato-cranialis anterior, onto Meckel's cartilage — so they are not scored here. This is a metamorphic shift of attachment inside one species, which is a different thing from the between-species shifts the rest of this dataset diffs.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae externus (pars superficialis, media, profunda), pseudotemporalis, zygomaticomandibularis, adductor mandibulae posterior
occurrences.origin: Temporal region — the emarginated or fully roofed temporal skull, with the trochlear redirection over the otic capsule (the turtle-specific pulley).
occurrences.insertion: Coronar aponeurosis and the medial and dorsal surfaces of the lower jaw.
occurrences.action: Jaw adduction; the trochlear arrangement redirects the muscle line of action over the otic process.
occurrences.note: Werneburg (2011) resolves this complex into discrete muscular units, each with its own innervation pattern, and supplies an exhaustive synonym list keyed to the historical literature back to Bojanus (1819–21).

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae (levator mandibulae externus, longus, articularis)
occurrences.note: Ascaphus truei, dissected by Johnston (2011) alongside Leiopelma. The innervation pattern — whether branches pass lateral or medial to the trigeminal ganglion — is the criterion the older literature used, and Johnston replaces it with insertion geometry: the components are identified by where they insert into the inverted U on the mandible.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae complex (externus, posterior, pseudotemporalis, pterygoideus)
occurrences.divisionNote: Columba livia. Jones et al. resolve four separate adductors, three of them further divided, and they disagree with earlier work on the boundaries: the m. AMEP is separable from the m. adductor mandibulae posterior on both sides of their specimen (contra van Gennip 1986), and the posterior is clearly separate from the pseudotemporalis profundus, unlike the arrangement reported for Columba palumbus. They also record that the homology of the externus partes across amniotes has been questioned outright, which is the same caution Johnston (2011, 2014) raises for this complex.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia, 242 g adult, from contrast-enhanced CT. The union of the four adductors' attachments; each component's own row carries the detail. Note what is NOT here: the separate postorbital bone is absent in birds, so the postorbital and zygomatic PROCESSES that carry part of the externus origin are recorded on the squamosal rather than on a postorbital element.
occurrences.note: In this specimen the externus lies lateral to both the maxillary (CN V2) and mandibular (CN V3) divisions, and the pseudotemporalis profundus bifurcates around CN V3 near its insertion — the nerve's course through the complex is what the CT dataset adds to the older dissections.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae (continuous block)
occurrences.note: Leiopelma hochstetteri, Johnston's primary animal — four specimens against two of Ascaphus, and the fuller description of the two. The group is a continuous block of muscle with no distinct separation into individual muscles, apart from a plane between the adductor mandibulae posterior and the rest, and a separate lateralis. That is the folded-sheet model's central claim made visible: the components are not separate muscles but named limbs of one sheet, identified by where each inserts into the inverted U around the posterior's insertion.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae anterior + posterior
occurrences.note: Hydrolagus colliei. Anderson's muscle group #1, the one group present and unambiguously homologous in all five gnathostomes he compares.

homology.notes: The single most robust cranial homology in Gnathostomata. Trigeminal innervation is invariant, and the muscle is present wherever jaws are. Subdivision patterns vary enormously and carry no homology weight on their own; the individual named parts are frequently non-homologous between clades even when the names match. Johnston (2011, 2014) resolves this complex into a folded sheet whose components are identified by where they insert into an inverted U wrapped around the adductor mandibulae posterior; those components are recorded separately here. Miyashita (2016) sets out the mandibular-confinement hypothesis for the origin of the jaw, which is the background for why cyclostome feeding musculature is not homologised with this complex despite both being trigeminal and mandibular-arch derived.
homology.teaching: Establish CN V = arch 1 = jaw closing first, then show that the mammalian masseter/temporalis split is a rearrangement within an ancient field, not a new muscle system.

consensus.origin: Medial surface of one mandibular ramus.
consensus.insertion: A midline raphe, or the contralateral ramus.
consensus.action: Raises the floor of the mouth; compresses the buccal cavity. Central to suction feeding and to buccal pumping.

occurrences.name: Intermandibularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias, from Huber et al.'s descriptions. A thin sheet between the two halves of the lower jaw, right and left portions inserting on the midventral raphe. It elevates the floor of the mouth during feeding and respiration, driving hydraulic transport through the oropharyngeal cavity. **Neither end is skeletal at the midline** — the insertion is raphe, which is why this muscle leaves no correlate.

occurrences.name: Intermandibularis
occurrences.note: Described for Arius by Jayaram et al. (1983), alongside the protractor hyoidei.

occurrences.name: Intermandibularis anterior + posterior
occurrences.divisionNote: Ambystoma mexicanum. Two muscles with a clear gap between them. The anterior is the one muscle in the head whose development is always delayed relative to the others — not visible until the end of stage 38, where the rest of the mandibular arch is already banded muscle cells.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma mexicanum, adult. The anterior stretches between the most anterior medial faces of the dentary; the posterior runs from the dentary to the median raphe, covering the anterior ventral half of the head. Both meet their contralateral partner in the raphe, and the posterior develops FROM its origin at Meckel's cartilage TOWARD that insertion, its fibres turning from posteromedial to latero-medial by stage 40. Two of the three taxa scored on this record now end at a raphe rather than on bone — the shark in Huber et al. and the pigeon in Jones et al. are the others — so the muscle's medial end is invisible to osteological reconstruction across gnathostomes, not just in one clade.

occurrences.name: Intermandibularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Werneburg resolves a pars principalis and a further unit; both run from the medial dentary to the midline.

occurrences.name: Mylohyoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. From the lingual edge of the dorsal ridge of the lower jaw into the median raphe. The same arrangement Huber et al. describe in Squalus: a sheet slung between the two rami whose midline end is a raphe and not a bone. Two of the three taxa now scored on this record insert on a raphe, which is the reason this muscle is invisible to osteological reconstruction at its medial end regardless of clade.

occurrences.name: Intermandibularis
occurrences.note: Hydrolagus colliei. Present in every taxon Anderson (2008) examines, stretching between the sides of the mandible on CN V. In the elasmobranchs it is continuous with the superficial constrictors; in Hydrolagus and the osteichthyans it is separate, which is the topological difference his group #3 has to absorb.

homology.notes: Present across Gnathostomata with invariant trigeminal innervation. The mammalian derivatives (tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, anterior digastric) illustrate the point better than any limb example: a muscle that ends up inside the ear still carries CN V.
homology.teaching: Pair the tensor tympani (CN V, arch 1) with the stapedius (CN VII, arch 2) — two tiny muscles millimetres apart in the middle ear, from different arches, with different nerves. The best available proof that arch identity is durable.

consensus.origin: Posterior skull roof — squamosal, otic region, or the hyomandibula.
consensus.insertion: Retroarticular process of the lower jaw.

occurrences.name: Constrictor hyoideus dorsalis (levator hyomandibulae)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias, from Huber et al.'s descriptions. Recorded here as the levator hyomandibulae, which originates on the otic capsule of the chondrocranium and on the epibranchial musculature. The dorsal and ventral hyoid constrictors insert on the tendinous sheath overlying the hyomandibular cartilage, the dorsal arising from the otic capsule and the cucullaris and the ventral alongside the interhyoideus on the raphe of the first gill slit.

occurrences.name: Depressor mandibulae (with levator hyoideus integrated)
occurrences.divisionNote: Ambystoma mexicanum, adult. Scored single because the levator hyoideus is not present as a distinct muscle in the adult — it is integrated into the depressor mandibulae. The ceratomandibularis is the other member of this complex, and its state across urodeles is genuinely variable: a distinct muscle in some obligate neotenes, completely fused to the branchiohyoideus and/or the depressor mandibulae in others, and missing in others again.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma mexicanum. Two insertions on two different bones, because two muscles fused: the depressor mandibulae proper attaches to Meckel's cartilage in the larva and the dentary in the adult, while at stage 44 some medial fibres of the complex still reach the ceratohyal in a steep angle, which is what makes those recognisable as the levator hyoideus. The otic-capsule origin is the levator hyoideus's — Ziermann & Diogo define that muscle by an origin on the otic capsule and an insertion on the ceratohyal — carried here because the two are one muscle in the adult. The fibre orientations still separate them from stage 43: dorsal fibres more vertical, ventral fibres more diagonal. The branchiohyoideus shares the same anlage and runs from the ceratobranchial around behind the jaw joint to the ceratohyal; it has no record of its own here.

occurrences.name: Depressor mandibulae anterior + posterior
occurrences.divisionNote: Necturus maculosus, adult. Two separate muscles, against ONE in the axolotl on the same record — where the levator hyoideus is integrated into an undivided depressor mandibulae. The names come from the constantly divided depressor of adult bolitoglossine plethodontids, all of which develop directly; Bauer's nomenclatural remarks trace 'depressor mandibulae' back to Humphry (1871), who used it for only the caudal part of the muscle in a metamorphosed Andrias.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Necturus maculosus, adult. The anterior arises along the lateral surface of the upper half of the squamosal and, ventral to that, on the otic capsule — the prootic, the opisthotic and the cartilage between them — inserting on the gonial, some rostrolateral fibres reaching the bone directly and most attaching to a tendon that is continuous with the ceratomandibularis tendon. The posterior arises caudal and medioventral to it on the caudalmost squamosal, the opisthotic and the same cartilage, and inserts through a long broad tendon on the posteromedial gonial; that tendon begins level with the dorsal tip of the ceratohyal and is slightly longer than the belly. TWO EARLIER DESCRIPTIONS ARE CORRECTED HERE AND NEITHER IS SCORED: there are no fibres on the parietal, against Fischer (1864), and no origins on the neck vertebrae, against Ruge (1897). Kesteven (1942-45) also put the whole posterior insertion on the ceratohyal, which Bauer finds among urodeles only in Siren.

occurrences.name: Depressor mandibulae
occurrences.note: Xenopus laevis, the anuran of Ziermann & Diogo's (2013) developmental series. The row previously claimed a leiopelmatid, which that paper does not examine.

occurrences.name: Depressor mandibulae
occurrences.origin: Posterolateral skull, dorsally from the quadrate.
occurrences.attachmentNote: One to two heads from the caudal, lateral and dorsal squamosal, occasionally the quadrate or quadratojugal; inserts partly by tendon on the posterior and ventral articular and the retroarticular process. Werneburg lists 13 synonyms for this muscle alone.

occurrences.name: Depressor mandibulae
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. From a broad area on the posterolateral surface of the squamosal, and also from the posterior and lateral surface of the postorbital ligament — a soft-tissue origin that leaves no bony trace. It inserts over a broad continuous area of the lower jaw: the dorsolateral corner, the flat posterior surface, and the posterior end of the medial surface. No landmark is asserted, because that area is wider than the retroarticular process this record's consensus names. Jones et al. add that because the quadrate is mobile, contracting it can protract the upper jaw as well as rotate the lower — one muscle acting on both jaws.

homology.notes: Jaw opening is an arch 2 (CN VII) function, jaw closing an arch 1 (CN V) function, throughout Gnathostomata. The digastric preserves both in one named muscle.
homology.teaching: The digastric is the cleanest single dissection for making the arch system tangible — one muscle, two nerves, two arches, one tendon.

consensus.origin: Hyoid arch elements (ceratohyal, hyomandibula) or the associated fascia.
consensus.insertion: Midline raphe of the throat, or the skin.
consensus.action: Constricts the pharyngeal floor; in mammals, moves the facial skin.

occurrences.name: Constrictor hyoideus ventralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias, from Huber et al.'s descriptions. A thin sheet lying dorsal to the intermandibularis, from the ceratohyal cartilages of the hyoid arch onto the midventral raphe, elevating the floor of the mouth. The hyoid-arch counterpart of the intermandibularis, and it shares its insertion.

occurrences.name: Interhyoideus (anterior + posterior)
occurrences.divisionNote: Ambystoma mexicanum. A thin anterior and a thicker posterior part whose border is not always clear, which is why this is `heads` and not `divided`. They develop in that order, anterior before posterior.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma mexicanum, adult. From the ceratohyal to the median raphe. The reason this row matters more than its two elements suggest is Ziermann & Diogo's Fig. 3C: in the adult all the superficial ventral muscles are fused into ONE THIN SHEET, and can only be divided by their origins — the mandible for the intermandibularis posterior, the ceratohyal for the interhyoideus. The attachment is not merely where the muscle ends; here it is the only thing that makes two muscles two.

occurrences.name: Constrictor colli / interhyoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: The constrictor colli complex, six units in Werneburg's scheme. Its spread from the hyoid onto the posterior skull is the sheet that in mammals becomes the facial musculature.

occurrences.name: Serpihyoideus + stylohyoideus
occurrences.divisionNote: Columba livia. Two CN VII bellies from the same hyoid-arch sheet, distinguished by where they end: the serpihyoideus at the midline, the stylohyoideus on the hyoid skeleton.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. Serpihyoideus from the posterodorsal surface of the lower jaw to the midline; stylohyoideus from the posterodorsal region of the lower jaw, underlapped medially by the serpihyoideus, onto the lateral surface of the basihyale. The split ends of one sheet are what makes this record's mammalian synonyms — platysma, stylohyoid — legible: the same sheet, ending on skin in one clade and on the hyoid in another.

occurrences.note: No homologous interhyoideus in Hydrolagus colliei, against its presence in the other four gnathostomes Anderson (2008) compares — Amia, Latimeria, Squalus and Chlamydoselachus — so he reads a secondary loss in chimaeroids. Recorded as `no` for this species only; the holocephalan sample here is one animal.

homology.notes: The transformation of a pharyngeal constrictor sheet into the mammalian facial musculature is tracked by constant CN VII innervation. This is arguably the most dramatic functional relocation of any vertebrate muscle field.
homology.teaching: Directly clinically relevant: explains why Bell's palsy affects the whole hemiface plus the stapedius (hyperacusis) but spares chewing (CN V, arch 1).

muscles.name: Ceratomandibularis
muscles.developmental: Hyoid arch. Bauer's point is neurological: it is supplied by the facial nerve, which places it in arch 2 with the depressor mandibulae and against the branchial muscles it lies among.

consensus.origin: Anterior surface of the first ceratobranchial.
consensus.insertion: The hyomandibular ligament, and through it the gonial; some fibres to the dorsal ceratohyal and some fused with the depressor mandibulae posterior.
consensus.action: Opens the jaw, pulling the lower jaw down against the hyobranchial apparatus rather than against the skull.

occurrences.name: Ceratomandibularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Necturus maculosus, adult. Origin on the upper two-thirds of the anterior surface of the first ceratobranchial, sparing the dorsalmost region, dorsal to the ceratohyoideus externus. Most of it inserts onto the HYOMANDIBULAR LIGAMENT together with the depressor mandibulae posterior, and so reaches the gonial only INDIRECTLY — the gonial row is that indirect attachment and the ligament row is the direct one, which is the distinction the two elements exist to keep. Two fibre bundles fuse with the depressor mandibulae posterior outright, and the ventralmost fibres attach to the caudal surface of the upturned dorsal end of the ceratohyal, just above where the ceratohyoideus externus ends.
occurrences.note: Necturus maculosus, adult, and Bauer's contrast is with every urodele larva and with Proteus: in those the ceratomandibularis is simple, while in Necturus it is HIGHLY COMPLEX, partly split by the fascia of origin of the interhyoideus posterior, whose medial layer pierces the muscle. He adds something no earlier worker reported — its deep fibres INTERMINGLE with those of the ceratohyoideus externus in two places, caudally where both attach to the ceratobranchial and rostrally near the posteroventral ceratohyal, while superficially the two are thoroughly separate. A muscle boundary that exists at the surface and not in depth.

homology.notes: A jaw opener that pulls against the hyobranchial apparatus rather than the skull, and the reason the urodele jaw-opening system cannot be read as one muscle. Its state across urodeles is genuinely variable: Ziermann & Diogo (2013) report it as a distinct muscle in some obligate neotenes, completely fused to the branchiohyoideus and/or the depressor mandibulae in others, and missing altogether in others — and where it fuses with the depressor mandibulae, the levator hyoideus is fused there too. So an absence in this record may be a loss or may be a fusion, and no source here separates the two for any species but this one.
homology.openQuestion: Is the ceratomandibularis absent or merely fused in the urodeles reported to lack it? Bauer's fibre-level observation in Necturus — superficial separation with deep intermingling — suggests the question may not have a clean answer at the level of gross dissection.
homology.teaching: The counterexample to 'jaw opening is the depressor mandibulae'. Here two CN VII muscles open the jaw, one from the skull and one from the gill skeleton, and only one of them reaches the jaw directly.

muscles.name: Stapedius / depressor hyomandibulae
muscles.developmental: Second pharyngeal arch mesoderm — the same arch as the stapes/hyomandibula it acts on.

consensus.action: Damps stapedial movement, attenuating loud sound.

occurrences.name: Depressor hyomandibulae
occurrences.note: Acts on the hyomandibula in its original role as a jaw suspensory element. The animal is Leucoraja erinacea, not the dogfish this row named for several passes: Ziermann et al. describe the muscle only in the little skate, and their discussion of its development from the hyoid condensation is explicitly about batoids. Their Squalus acanthias hyoid section lists an interhyoideus, a constrictor hyoideus dorsalis and an adductor arcus palatini, and no depressor. Whether a selachian has one is a question this source does not answer, so it is not scored as an absence either.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leucoraja erinacea. Insertion onto the hyomandibula and onto the horizontal tendon associated with it. No origin row — both heads arise from fascia, one at the contact with the contralateral muscle over the coracomandibularis and one on the fascia overlying the sternohyoideus, so the muscle that becomes the mammalian stapedius begins its recorded history attached to the element at one end and to nothing skeletal at the other.

homology.notes: The hyomandibula→stapes transformation is one of the best-documented in vertebrate evolution, and the muscle acting on it tracked the element throughout. The spiracular sequence of Gai et al. (2022) is the skeletal counterpart of this muscle's history: the pouch it sits beside becomes the tympanic cavity.
homology.teaching: Teach with the tensor tympani. Two middle-ear muscles, two arches, two nerves, both retained through a wholesale change of function.

consensus.origin: Branchial arch elements and the adjacent fascia.
consensus.insertion: Adjacent branchial elements and the midline raphe.
consensus.action: Compress and expand the branchial chamber for gill ventilation; in tetrapods, swallowing and vocalisation.
consensus.innervation: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) for arch 3; vagus nerve (CN X) for arches 4–7.

occurrences.name: Constrictor branchiarum (+ constrictor pharyngis)
occurrences.note: Hagfish branchial musculature is difficult to homologise cell-for-cell with the gnathostome series; Oisi et al. (2013) provide the developmental basis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Myxine glutinosa, and the row is mostly a record of what is NOT bone. Ziermann et al. give the constrictor branchiarum an origin on the mesentery and insertions onto the connective tissue around the efferent branchial ducts, the surface of the heart, and the fascia of the branchial pouches — not one skeletal attachment among them. Only the anterior fibres, the constrictor pharyngis, reach cartilage: they arise from the lateral tissue of the chorda, which is tissue beside the notochord rather than the notochord itself and so is left unscored, and insert on the lateral borders of the posterior lingual cartilages. A branchial constrictor that ends on the heart and the tongue skeleton is the strongest single argument in this record against reading the hagfish series as the gnathostome one.

occurrences.name: Constrictores branchiales externi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Petromyzon marinus. The muscle is a single external sheet wrapped around the outside of the branchial basket and divided into seven segments by the cartilages and the gill openings, so its attachments are to the longitudinal bars of the basket rather than to any one arch: the fibres run ventrally to the taenia longitudinalis ventralis, and the medial portion lies beneath the epitrematica and hypotrematica. Scored on `taenia-longitudinalis` by side, dorsal for the epitrematica. No origin row — the sheet arises from the basket's own segmental cartilages along its whole length, which is a field rather than a site. External to the gills is the point: the gnathostome constrictors lie inside them.

occurrences.name: Constrictores + levatores arcuum branchialium
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias, from Huber et al.'s descriptions. The superficial branchial constrictors take origin from the tendinous intersections between the dorsal and ventral series and insert on each of the gill slits, compressing the pharynx during the expulsion phase. Scored at the arch and the slit: the tendinous intersections are the real proximal attachment and have no element.

occurrences.name: Branchial musculature
occurrences.note: Lepisosteus osseus, the longnose gar. Naumann et al. trace the development of the branchial muscles and the cucullaris and find they share a cranial mesoderm source. The row previously named a catfish, which they do not examine.

occurrences.name: Dorsal and ventral gill-arch muscles
occurrences.innervation: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and vagus nerve (CN X).

parts.name: Recti dorsales 1-4
parts.note: Among elopomorphs only Protanguilla has a rectus dorsalis 4 — one of the nine anguilliform synapomorphies this paper identifies.

parts.name: Rectus 4
parts.note: Small in most eels the authors examined but well developed here, and easily mistaken for the R4Cm this species lacks.

occurrences.divisionNote: Protanguilla palau. Fifteen units present, which makes this the most divided this record is in any taxon — the gill basket of a fish against ten units in the axolotl and eight in the pigeon. What is ABSENT matters as much: obliquus dorsalis 3, adductores 1-3, recti 1 and 2, and R4Cm are all recorded absent in this species, and the authors use those absences and presences as characters — nine anguilliform synapomorphies, seven of them myological and all but two reported for the first time.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Protanguilla palau, USNM 396051. The dorsal series: each levator externus arises on the cranium — Springer & Johnson note the exact position was not recorded, which is why the origin row is the neurocranium with no landmark — and inserts on the lateral third of its own epibranchial. The levatores interni insert on the pharyngobranchials, LI2 bifurcating onto Pb3 and the fourth upper pharyngeal toothplate. The recti dorsales run epibranchial to PRECEDING epibranchial, which is the arrangement that needed resolved elements to express at all. RecD1's insertion was lost when the gill arches were removed and is inferred from Anguilla to have been the dorsal tip of the posterior ceratohyal — that is the ceratohyal row, and it is an inference inside an otherwise directly observed set. The ventral series runs ceratobranchial to hypobranchial: ObV1 Cb1 to Hb1, ObV2 Cb2 to Hb2, R3 Cb3 to Hb2, R4 Cb4 to an elongate CARTILAGINOUS Hb3. Ceratobranchial is scored as `cornu-branchiale`, the dataset's record for that element, whose presence list this pass extends to the ray-finned fishes.
occurrences.note: Protanguilla palau. The paper's purpose is phylogenetic — it corroborates anguilliform monophyly and supports Protanguilla as sister to all other eels — so the muscle attachments here are characters first and anatomy second. Two are worth carrying: only this species has a rectus dorsalis 4 among elopomorphs, and a cartilaginous or absent hypobranchial 3 is an anguilliform synapomorphy, that element being largely ossified in all other elopomorphs and most other teleosts.

occurrences.name: Levatores arcuum branchialium I-IV, subarcuales, levatores and depressores branchiarum, transversus ventralis IV
occurrences.innervation: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and vagus nerve (CN X).
occurrences.divisionNote: Ambystoma mexicanum. Ten units, which makes this the most divided this record is in any taxon and is what a functioning gill apparatus costs. The dorsal levatores develop before the true ventral branchial muscles.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma mexicanum. The levatores arcuum branchialium I-IV arise from the fascia cephalodorsalis covering the otic capsule, lateral to the epaxial muscles, each inserting on its own ceratobranchial — a fascial origin, so the otic-capsule row is the bone the fascia covers rather than the attachment itself. The ventral series is ceratobranchial-to-ceratobranchial and ceratobranchial-to-hyoid: subarcualis rectus I runs from ceratobranchial I to the ceratohyal in larva and adult alike, subarcualis rectus II-IV from ceratobranchial IV medially onto ceratobranchial I and ventrally onto II and III, and the subarcuales obliqui II and III arise from their own ceratobranchials and fuse before inserting together on the basibranchial. The levatores and depressores branchiarum I-III arise from the commissurae terminales, which are cartilage bars with no element here. Ceratobranchial is scored as `cornu-branchiale` and basibranchial as `corpus-hyoidei`, the dataset's names for those elements.

occurrences.name: Levator + depressor laryngis, constrictor laryngis, dilatator laryngis
occurrences.note: Werneburg (2011) documents the laryngeal muscles as branchial-arch derivatives with distinct innervation.

homology.notes: Arch-by-arch innervation is preserved from cyclostomes to mammals. The reduction of the posterior arch series in tetrapods leaves the pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles as the surviving remnants of a gill-ventilation system. Higashiyama et al. (2016) document the branchial and intestinal portions of the vagus and their cardiac branches, which is the innervation context for the posterior arch series.
homology.teaching: The stylopharyngeus is a memorable single fact: one muscle, one nerve, one arch, the last of its kind.

muscles.name: Extraocular muscles
muscles.developmental: Prechordal plate and cranial paraxial mesoderm — NOT pharyngeal arch derived. Distinct from every other cranial muscle group in origin.
synonyms: rectus superior / inferior / medialis (internus, nasalis) / lateralis (externus)

consensus.origin: Around the optic foramen and the orbital wall.
consensus.action: Rotate the eye about three axes; retractor bulbi withdraws the globe.
consensus.innervation: Oculomotor (CN III): rectus superior, inferior, medialis, obliquus inferior, levator palpebrae. Trochlear (CN IV): obliquus superior. Abducens (CN VI): rectus lateralis, retractor bulbi.

occurrences.note: Myxine glutinosa has no extraocular muscles at all, and no ocular motor neurons to supply them — on Fritzsch's compilation the only vertebrate group of which that is true. The eyes themselves are reduced. This is an absence with a mechanism rather than a failure to find the muscle, which is what makes it scoreable as `no` rather than left unrecorded, and it is the floor of the record: lampreys already have six.

occurrences.name: Extraocular muscles
occurrences.note: Petromyzon marinus has a full set of six extraocular muscles on three nerves, establishing that the system predates jaws. The assignments are not the gnathostome ones: three on CN III, one on CN IV, two on CN VI, with a caudal rectus that gnathostomes lose and no medial rectus, which is a tetrapod and coelacanth addition. Sourced to Fritzsch, not to Ziermann et al. — that paper contains no extraocular content and was cited here in error.

occurrences.name: Extraocular muscles
occurrences.innervation: CN III, IV and CN VI, but not the crown-osteichthyan pattern.
occurrences.note: Squalus acanthias, and the chondrichthyan set is neither the lamprey's nor the tetrapod's. Fritzsch gives elasmobranchs and lungfish a contralateral nasal rectus on a dorsal ramus of CN III that crown osteichthyans lack, and no medial rectus; the caudal rectus of lampreys is already gone. The earlier reading of this row as 'the standard gnathostome pattern' flattened two differences in both directions.

occurrences.name: Rectus superior, inferior, anterior, posterior; obliquus superior, inferior; retractor bulbi; ciliaris; sphincter and dilatator pupillae; transversalis oculi
occurrences.origin: Around the optic foramen and the anterodorsal corner of the optic cavity.
occurrences.insertion: Eyeball; the ciliary and iridial muscles onto intraocular structures.
occurrences.innervation: CN III for rectus anterior, inferior, superior, obliquus inferior, ciliaris, dilatator and sphincter pupillae, transversalis oculi; CN IV for obliquus superior.
occurrences.note: Werneburg (2011) records ten distinct ocular muscular units in turtles, including intraocular muscles absent from most vertebrate accounts. Turtles (like birds) have striated intraocular muscles, so pupillary control is partly voluntary.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eight units around the optic foramen and the anterodorsal optic cavity, all inserting on the eyeball. Werneburg additionally records intraocular muscles (ciliaris, sphincter and dilatator pupillae, transversalis oculi) that most vertebrate accounts omit; turtles, like birds, have striated intraocular muscle.

occurrences.name: Four recti, two obliqui, three levatores palpebrae, pyramidalis and quadratus
occurrences.innervation: Oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV) and abducens (CN VI).

parts.name: Levator palpebrae obliquus
parts.note: Jones et al.'s survey of columbiform accounts has it present in some and absent or unreported in others.

occurrences.divisionNote: Columba livia. The recti and obliqui are the conserved six; what is added in birds is the nictitating-membrane apparatus (pyramidalis and quadratus) and up to three levatores palpebrae. The retractor bulbi, which this record notes for mammals, is not among them.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. The recti arise from a thickened periorbital membrane around the orbital wall and insert on the sclera by quadrant — dorsalis posterodorsal, ventralis anteroventral, medialis anterodorsal, lateralis posteroventral. The obliqui arise from the anterior and anterodorsal orbital wall. The periorbital membrane is worth noting: several of these origins are on connective tissue rather than bone, so the orbit rows are the bony frame of the origin and not the origin itself.

homology.notes: The most conserved muscle group in the vertebrate head: same six muscles, same three nerves, from lampreys to mammals. Their non-branchiomeric origin makes them the exception that defines the arch system — they are the cranial muscles that are not arch muscles. Fritzsch (2023) adds the one mammalian wrinkle: the retractor bulbi is retained in many mammals and lost in humans and other primates, so the six-muscle count is a primate simplification of a seven-muscle plan.
homology.teaching: Use as the control case. If cranial muscle homology were merely a matter of position, the extraocular muscles would not be so much more stable than the arch muscles; their stability is a consequence of a developmentally distinct and functionally rigid system.
homology.caveat: Fritzsch (2023) is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed. Cite the primary sources it points to rather than the preprint itself.

muscles.name: Hypobranchial muscles
muscles.developmental: Occipital and anterior trunk somites. The myoblasts migrate forward beneath the pharynx, which is why they are somitic muscles in a cranial position — and why the hypoglossal nerve, a spinal nerve in origin, ends up cranial.

consensus.action: Depress the hyoid and the lower jaw; protrude and shape the tongue. In fishes, expand the buccal cavity for suction feeding.
consensus.innervation: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) and the ansa cervicalis (C1–C3) — spinal in origin, not branchiomeric.

occurrences.name: Hypobranchial musculature
occurrences.note: Present in Petromyzon marinus but with a different arrangement; the lamprey lingual apparatus is not homologous to the gnathostome tongue. Left unscored deliberately rather than for want of a pass: Ziermann et al. describe the obliquus and decussatus as ending on a median raphe and on their contralateral partners, the rectus as continuous with the sphincter cloacae, and the hypobranchialis as a segmented muscle continuous with the parietalis behind and the subocularis in front. Not one skeletal attachment in the set. Where the shark's hypobranchial series runs from the coracoid bar to the mandible, hyoid and branchial arches, the lamprey's runs muscle-to-muscle, and copying the shark's rows here would assert an observation nobody made.

occurrences.name: Coracomandibularis, coracohyoideus, coracobranchialis
occurrences.origin: Coracoid bar of the pectoral girdle.
occurrences.action: Depress the jaw and hyoid, expanding the orobranchial chamber for suction feeding.
occurrences.innervation: Ventral rami of the occipital and anterior spinal nerves.
occurrences.note: The coracoid origin makes the mechanical link between the pectoral girdle and the feeding apparatus explicit — the same link that must be broken for a neck to evolve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin on the coracoid bar ties the feeding apparatus mechanically to the pectoral girdle. Loosening that link is a precondition for a neck.

occurrences.name: Geniohyoideus, sternohyoideus, omohyoideus
occurrences.innervation: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) and the cervical spinal nerves.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma mexicanum. The geniohyoideus develops from its origin at the basibranchial toward its insertion on Meckel's cartilage and/or the dentary, close to the origin of the intermandibularis anterior; in the adult it widens and closes the gap between the contralateral pair. The sternohyoideus is blended posteriorly with the RECTUS ABDOMINIS — the clearest statement in the corpus that this group is trunk muscle that migrated forward — and inserts on the hypobranchial, dorsally on the basibranchial and medially on the rostral end of ceratobranchial I. The omohyoideus derives ontogenetically from the sternohyoideus, stays deeply blended with it, and extends posterolaterally to the pectoral girdle, which is the girdle end of the link whose loosening Diogo & Ziermann tie to the origin of the neck.

occurrences.name: Geniohyoideus, coracohyoideus, genioglossus, hyoglossus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Aggregated across eight units (genioglossus, geniohyoideus, coracohyoideus, hyoglossus and their parts). Werneburg records CN XII for these, confirming their somitic rather than branchiomeric origin.

occurrences.name: Genioglossus, hypoglossus, cricohyoideus, sternohyoideus, branchiomandibularis
occurrences.innervation: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) and the cervical spinal nerves.
occurrences.divisionNote: Columba livia. Eight bellies, which is the most divided this record is in any taxon. Jones et al. treat the ceratohyoideus with the throat series; it is included here as a part rather than given its own row because no source in this dataset separates it as a homology group.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. The tongue and throat series, running between the mandible, the tongue skeleton and the sternum: genioglossus anterior from near the mandibular symphysis onto the floor of the mouth; hypoglossus rectus from the ventral paraglossum onto the anterior entoglossum, obliquus from the ventral edge of the paraglossum; cricohyoideus and sternohyoideus both onto the posterior paraglossum and the dorsal hyoid, the latter from the sternum. The sternal origin is the point of comparison with the shark, where the same field arises from the coracoid bar: what loosened that girdle-to-tongue link is what allowed a neck.
occurrences.note: Somitic rather than branchiomeric, which is what CN XII records.

occurrences.name: Coracomandibularis + coracohyoideus + mandibulohyoideus
occurrences.note: Hydrolagus colliei, and the record's most interesting column. Anderson (2008) finds a coracomandibularis in all five gnathostomes and argues from it that basal jaw depression was NOT coupled to hyoid movement but worked directly through this muscle — the osteichthyan coracohyoideus-through-mandibulohyoid-ligament system being the derived arrangement. He also renames a Hydrolagus muscle called geniohyoideus by some authors and interhyoideus by others to `mandibulohyoideus`, because it matches neither and is apomorphic. Its consequence is that Hydrolagus has TWO ways to depress the jaw, the chondrichthyan coracomandibularis and a geniohyoideus-like mandibulohyoideus, which Anderson raises as possible independent acquisition of an osteichthyan-style depression in chimaeroids.

occurrences.name: Coracomandibularis + coracohyoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Callorhinchus milii. A very large coracomandibularis with its main origin on the T-shaped anteroventral face of the coracoid region of the pectoral girdle, inserting along Meckel's cartilage — triangular in ventral view, broadening forwards. This is the muscle Anderson (2008) finds in all five gnathostomes he compares and argues from: basal jaw depression pulled on the mandible directly from the girdle, and was not coupled to the hyoid. Scoring it here puts the same attachment in a holocephalan and a selachian.

homology.notes: The hypobranchial muscles are somitic muscles in the head, and this is exactly what CN XII records — it is a fused series of occipital spinal nerves, not a true cranial nerve of the branchiomeric type. Diogo & Ziermann (2015) connect the loosening of the coracoid-to-mandible link with the origin of the vertebrate neck. Two mammalian details, previously carried by a row attributed to a cheetah that no source dissected: the palatoglossus is the exception that confirms the rule, being the only 'tongue' muscle on CN X because it is a soft-palate (arch 4) muscle rather than a hypobranchial one; and with the coracoid gone the infrahyoid muscles take origin from sternum, clavicle and scapula instead.
homology.teaching: Answers a question students always have: why does a nerve numbered among the twelve cranial nerves behave like a spinal nerve? Because it is one.

muscles.name: Levator arcus palatini / spiracular musculature
muscles.developmental: First pharyngeal arch mesoderm, dorsal division.

consensus.origin: Otic and postorbital region of the neurocranium.
consensus.insertion: Palatoquadrate or its derivatives; the spiracular region.
consensus.action: Elevates and abducts the palatoquadrate; controls the spiracle where one is present.

occurrences.name: Levator palatoquadrati, spiracularis
occurrences.note: The spiracle is the reduced first (mandibular) gill slit; its musculature is arch 1 and trigeminal.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias, from Huber et al.'s descriptions. Two muscles on this record. The levator palatoquadrati runs from the otic capsule of the chondrocranium onto the palatoquadrate, elevating the upper jaw into its resting position during the recovery phase of the gape cycle. The spiracularis inserts on the spiracular cartilage and the distal hyomandibula, forming the anterior wall of the spiracular valve.

occurrences.name: Levator arcus palatini, dilatator operculi
occurrences.action: Abducts the suspensorium during suction feeding.

occurrences.name: Protractor pterygoidei et quadrati
occurrences.note: Columba livia. Scored on this record as the amniote representative of the mandibular-arch dorsal division — the muscle that moves the palatoquadrate. The record's other rows are the shark's levator palatoquadrati and spiracularis and a catfish's; this is its first amniote row, and the identification rests on position and on CN V innervation rather than on any source here stating the homology outright, which is why it is worth saying so.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. From the posterior surface of the orbit, dividing into two heads: the dorsal inserts on the dorsal edge and posterior surface of the anteromedial process of the quadrate, the ventral onto the posterior surface of the pterygoid. Contraction protracts the pterygoid-quadrate-maxillopalatine complex and opens the UPPER jaw — the cranial kinesis that has no counterpart in the taxa this record's other rows come from.

occurrences.note: Absent in Hydrolagus colliei, and Anderson (2008) gives the reason rather than the fact: the holocephalan palatoquadrate is fused to the cranium (autostylic suspension), so there is no free element to levate. He reads it as a secondary loss — the muscle is basal for gnathostomes and went when the joint did. This is the cleanest case in the dataset of a muscle disappearing because its skeletal degree of freedom disappeared, and the counterpart of the coracoid loss that moves the therian supracoracoideus.

homology.notes:
The spiracular series is important for the origin of the tetrapod middle ear: the spiracular pouch is the ancestor of the tympanic cavity, and the mandibular-arch identity of the region is preserved by trigeminal innervation. Gai et al. (2022) trace the spiracular region from jawless fishes to tetrapods, which is the fossil evidence behind treating the spiracular pouch as antecedent to the tympanic cavity — a claim this record previously made without a source.

Distribution, as the sources give it: present in chondrichthyans and osteichthyans, and probably lost in holocephalans, which Ziermann & Diogo (2019) relate to the fusion of the palatoquadrate with the neurocranium in that clade (after Ziermann et al. 2014; Miyake et al. 1992; Anderson 2008). **No source here states the muscle's fate in mammals.** This record carried a *present: "no"* row for Acinonyx jubatus with no source and a guessed species, reasoning from suspensorium-to-braincase fusion — which is the holocephalan argument transplanted to a mammal by nobody in particular. The row is gone: an unobserved absence is unrecorded, not observed. Didier (1987), a holocephalan myology thesis already in `papers/`, is the way to turn the chimaera loss into a species-level row.
homology.teaching: Connects jaw suspension, gill slits and the middle ear in one developmental field.

muscles.name: Adductor mandibulae internus
muscles.subregion: mandibular arch — adductor complex, medial limb of the U

consensus.origin: Dorsal braincase medial to the orbit, and the pterygoid.
consensus.insertion: Mandible, medial to its articulation with the quadrate; via a flat tendon in anurans.
consensus.action: Adducts the mandible; the medial limb of the adductor sheet.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae internus (medial division)
occurrences.note: Callorhinchus milii, the holocephalan in Johnston's comparative material — his model of the adductor complex as a folded sheet was tested from chondrichthyans to mammals, and this is the cartilaginous fish he tested it on. The medial division is identified by where it inserts into the inverted U on the mandible.

occurrences.name: Pseudotemporalis
occurrences.divisionNote: Ambystoma mexicanum, adult. ONE undivided muscle, and that is the result rather than the starting point: the larva has a pseudotemporalis superficialis (the A3' of fishes) and a pseudotemporalis profundus (the A3''), the profundus visible from stage 39, and during larval development it becomes completely integrated into the main body of the muscle. A division event running backwards.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma mexicanum, adult. The origin has MOVED DORSALLY during development — dorsolateral on the palatoquadrate (orbital cartilage) in the larva, and in the adult from the midline of the parietal and caudally from the first vertebrae. That is a jaw muscle acquiring an axial origin, and it is why this row carries a vertebral element. Insertion caudodorsal on the dentary; in the larva both portions insert on Meckel's cartilage.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae internus (rostral + caudal parts)
occurrences.origin: Dorsal braincase medial to the eye; in Leiopelma the origin extends further rostrally than in Ascaphus or most other frogs.
occurrences.insertion: Mandible immediately medial to the quadrate–mandibular articulation, by a flat tendon.
occurrences.note: Two parts merging into one another. Johnston prefers 'adductor mandibulae' to 'levator mandibulae' for anurans, to align with usage across gnathostomes.

occurrences.name: Pseudotemporalis + pterygoideus
occurrences.divisionNote: Columba livia. Four bellies in two pairs. This record holds both the pseudotemporalis and the pterygoideus because both are internal adductors of one field — the same grouping Werneburg (2011) uses for turtles.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. Pseudotemporalis superficialis has a broad fleshy origin on the posterior wall of the orbit and inserts by aponeurosis at a narrow point on the lower jaw; profundus arises from a small region on the medialmost end of the medial process of the quadrate and inserts broadly on the lateral, dorsal and medial surfaces of the jaw anterior to the coronoid process, taking in most of the adductor fossa — and it bifurcates around CN V3 close to its insertion, which is how the nerve reaches the Meckelian groove. Pterygoideus dorsalis arises from the dorsolateral palatine (anterior part) and the lateral pterygoid (medial and posterior parts); Jones et al. see no part of the anterior head on the pterygoid, against Bhattacharyya. Pterygoideus ventralis arises from the posterolateral ventral palatine and the ventral pterygoid and inserts on the medial surface and posterolateral corner of the jaw. It matters most at large gapes — continuously active during drinking, and during the grasping phase of feeding.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae internus (rostral + caudal parts)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri, Johnston's primary animal — four specimens against two of Ascaphus, and the fuller description of the two. The rostral origin on the dorsal braincase medial to the eye extends further forward than in Ascaphus truei or in most other frogs, which is the species difference this row exists to hold — it had been carried as prose on the Ascaphus row. The rostral part converges on a flat tendon inserting immediately medial to the quadrate–mandibular articulation; the caudal part has a more ventral fibre direction and a fleshy insertion on the medial mandible beside that tendon.

homology.notes: Johnston (2011, 2014) models the adductor complex as a folded sheet whose insertion on the mandible forms an inverted U wrapped around the insertion of the adductor mandibulae posterior. Components are identified by WHERE THEY INSERT INTO THAT U, not by which side of a trigeminal branch they lie on — the criterion the older literature used and which does not survive comparison across gnathostomes. The pterygoideus is a separated component of the internus rather than an independent muscle.
homology.teaching: Use with the other components to show that a 'muscle' in the older literature is often one limb of a continuous sheet.

muscles.name: Adductor mandibulae longus
muscles.subregion: mandibular arch — adductor complex, dorsal limb of the U

consensus.insertion: Mandible, at the dorsal border, deep to the externus.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae externus profundus
occurrences.note: McDowell (1986) proposed that this component is ABSENT in colubroid snakes — one of the two moves that reconciles lizard and snake adductor anatomy.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri, Johnston's primary animal — four specimens against two of Ascaphus, and the fuller description of the two. Origin from the parietal region of the braincase and over the convexity of the otic capsule as far back as the dorsal and caudal limits of the skull, including the crista parotica. The fibres pass ventrally and rostrally, medial to the processus zygomaticus of the squamosal, to insert around the apex of the U on the coronoid area of the mandible. Johnston reports the same origin dorsal to the otic capsule in Ascaphus truei.

homology.notes: Johnston (2011, 2014) models the adductor complex as a folded sheet whose insertion on the mandible forms an inverted U wrapped around the insertion of the adductor mandibulae posterior. Components are identified by WHERE THEY INSERT INTO THAT U, not by which side of a trigeminal branch they lie on — the criterion the older literature used and which does not survive comparison across gnathostomes.
homology.openQuestion: Whether the profundus component is genuinely lost in colubroid snakes, as McDowell (1986) proposed and Johnston (2014) endorses, or merely rearranged.

muscles.name: Adductor mandibulae externus
muscles.subregion: mandibular arch — adductor complex, lateral limb of the U

consensus.insertion: Mandible, on and near its dorsolateral border.
consensus.action: Adducts the mandible; usually the bulkiest component.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae externus superficialis + medialis
occurrences.note: In lizards the components are layered lateral to medial; in macrostomatan snakes they appear layered rostral to caudal. Johnston (2014) shows the folded-sheet model reconciles the two.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae externus (pars superficialis, media, profunda)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Aggregated across the seven units Werneburg resolves (pars superficialis, media, profunda and their subdivisions). The wide origin over the skull roof and braincase, and the redirection of the line of action over the otic process, are what the turtle trochlear arrangement buys.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae externus (pars superficialis, medialis, profundus)
occurrences.divisionNote: Columba livia. Three distinct partes in this specimen, though in many birds the superficialis and medialis are hard to separate; the medialis is itself divided by an internal aponeurosis into anterior and posterior portions. Jones et al. note that whether these partes are homologous with those of other amniotes has been questioned.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. Pars superficialis from the lateral surface of the squamosal within the fossa temporalis, inserting by aponeurosis on a small region of the coronoid process. Pars medialis by three short aponeuroses — one from the postorbital process, two from the zygomatic process — with a broad fleshy insertion on the lateral surface of the lower jaw; Jones et al. follow van Gennip's three-part origin against the single zygomatic origin others report. Pars profundus from the dorsolateral part of the anterolateral surface of the quadrate onto a small point on the dorsal jaw behind the coronoid process. The postorbital and zygomatic processes are scored on the squamosal: birds have no separate postorbital bone, and `skeleton.json` records it as absent in Aves, so a row on it would be a validation error rather than an observation.
occurrences.note: Positionally diagnostic: in amniotes this muscle usually lies BETWEEN CN V2 and CN V3, and in Columba livia it lies lateral to both.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae externus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri, Johnston's primary animal — four specimens against two of Ascaphus, and the fuller description of the two. Contiguous laterally with the longus, and inserting as the lateral limb of the U. Origin on the squamosal and the quadrate.

homology.notes: Johnston (2011, 2014) models the adductor complex as a folded sheet whose insertion on the mandible forms an inverted U wrapped around the insertion of the adductor mandibulae posterior. Components are identified by WHERE THEY INSERT INTO THAT U, not by which side of a trigeminal branch they lie on — the criterion the older literature used and which does not survive comparison across gnathostomes. Snake adductors were long thought to have a different configuration from lizards; the difference is in the folding, not in the components. Werneburg & Preuschoft (2024) give the osteological side of this muscle: they treat the temporal bars as struts resisting the compressive and tensile stresses of biting, so the pattern of temporal openings is a consequence of where adductor force is transmitted rather than an arbitrary character. That makes the temporal configuration usable as evidence about adductor volume and orientation in fossils.
homology.teaching: The lizard-versus-snake case is a good demonstration that apparent reorganisation can be a change in geometry rather than in composition.

muscles.name: Adductor mandibulae lateralis
muscles.subregion: mandibular arch — adductor complex, outermost limb of the U

consensus.origin: Lateral surface of the temporal region.
consensus.insertion: Mandible, laterally, outside the externus insertion.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae lateralis
occurrences.note: Johnston (2011) recognises a separate lateralis in Leiopelma and Ascaphus, distinct from the externus.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae lateralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri, Johnston's primary animal — four specimens against two of Ascaphus, and the fuller description of the two. A small separate body at the most lateral and caudal extent of the group, arising from the quadrate just dorsal to its articulation with the mandible and passing ventral and rostral to lie lateral to V3. It is the one component Johnston finds genuinely separate from the block besides the posterior.

homology.notes: Johnston (2011, 2014) models the adductor complex as a folded sheet whose insertion on the mandible forms an inverted U wrapped around the insertion of the adductor mandibulae posterior. Components are identified by WHERE THEY INSERT INTO THAT U, not by which side of a trigeminal branch they lie on — the criterion the older literature used and which does not survive comparison across gnathostomes. Recognised as a discrete component in basal anurans; its identity elsewhere is not established.

muscles.name: Adductor mandibulae posterior
muscles.subregion: mandibular arch — the axis the U folds around

consensus.insertion: Mandible, at the centre of the inverted U formed by the other components.
consensus.action: Adducts the mandible; the axis of the folded sheet.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae posterior
occurrences.note: Callorhinchus milii, from Johnston's comparative material. The adductor mandibulae posterior is the component the inverted U of the other insertions wraps around, which is what makes it the landmark for identifying the rest.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Callorhinchus milii, from Dearden et al.'s synchrotron dissection. Origin along the anterior edge of the suborbital shelf, anteroventral to the orbit; insertion over a small angle on Meckel's cartilage, joining a sheet of connective tissue slung ventrally around it. The muscle's surface is divided in two by the passage of V3 — the same nerve-through-the-sheet geometry Johnston uses to argue this component is of different homology from the rest of the adductor group. Didier (1995) also reports a preorbital fascial origin that the scans do not show, so it is noted rather than scored.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: One to two heads arising anteromedially on the quadrate, medial to the adductor mandibulae externus; inserts partly directly and partly by its own tendon. Insertion on the articular puts it at the centre of the inverted U formed by the other components (Johnston 2011).
occurrences.note: Werneburg & Maier (2019) show the palatoquadrate this muscle arises from is fused to the braincase in turtles, and that cryptodires and pleurodires build that fixation differently — cryptodires via an ossified ascending process (the epipterygoid) bridged ventrally by the pterygoid, pleurodires by appositional bone of the quadrate with the parietal's descending process forming the braincase wall. The muscle's origin surface is therefore not developmentally the same structure in the two clades.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. From the ventral part of the anterolateral surface of the quadrate, ventromedial to the origin of the externus pars profundus, onto a flat triangular surface on the dorsal mandible immediately anterior to the jaw joint. Jones et al. find it reasonably distinct from the externus pars profundus (contra van Gennip 1986) and clearly separate from the pseudotemporalis profundus. Its size and position suggest it stabilises the jaws during closure and may assist opening — a function no in vivo recording has tested.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri, Johnston's primary animal — four specimens against two of Ascaphus, and the fuller description of the two. A cylindrical belly running from the anterior face of the quadrate to the dorsal mandible immediately rostral to the articulation. This is the axis the adductor sheet folds around, and Johnston's argument that it is of different homology from the rest of the group is what makes the remainder resolvable at all.

homology.notes: Johnston (2011, 2014) treats this as being of DIFFERENT homology from the rest of the adductor group. It is the axis the folded sheet wraps around, not one of its limbs, and separating it is what makes the rest of the complex resolvable.
homology.teaching: The single most important distinction in the complex: everything else folds around this.

consensus.origin: Temporal and orbital region, superficial to the adductor sheet.
consensus.insertion: Rictal plate (Mundplatte) at the corner of the mouth; in some snakes the venom gland or the mandible directly.
consensus.action: Draws the corner of the mouth; in snakes, involved in gape and in venom-gland mechanics.

occurrences.name: Levator anguli oris
occurrences.note: Newly defined in Ascaphus truei by Johnston (2011) — the first record of this muscle in a frog — and not found in Leiopelma hochstetteri, which now carries its own absent row. Presence was `variable` here for several passes, which was the clade's answer written onto one animal: Ascaphus either has the muscle or does not, and it has it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ascaphus truei. Arises from the dorsal surface of the palatal membrane in the triangular area between pterygoid and maxilla — the membrane is the actual origin and has no element, so the two bones bounding it are scored instead — wraps around the rostral border of the longus, and passes medial to the maxilla and the maxillo-quadrate ligament to insert on the rictal plate at the corner of the mouth. Johnston names it for the lepidosaur muscle because that insertion is the lepidosaur one; the same rictal plate is what becomes the venom gland in colubroid snakes on his 2014 reading.

occurrences.name: Levator anguli oris
occurrences.note: The most superficial layer of the typical lepidosaurian pattern, attaching to the rictal plate. McDowell (1986) identified the rostral 'external adductor' component of colubroid snakes as this muscle, modified around the venom gland — the second of the two moves reconciling lizard and snake anatomy.

Absent in Leiopelma hochstetteri. Johnston (2011) identifies the muscle in Ascaphus truei — the first record of a levator anguli oris in any frog — and does not find it in Leiopelma, so the two basal anuran lineages differ and Anura computes as variable rather than being declared so.

homology.notes: Its identification is the crux of the lizard–snake problem. In colubroid snakes the rictal plate becomes the venom gland, so parts of the muscle insert on the gland or straight onto the mandible instead.
homology.openQuestion: Johnston (2014) notes that authors after McDowell (1986) neither adopted nor extended his model; the homology is endorsed here but is not consensus.
homology.teaching: A muscle whose insertion target itself evolved into a novel organ — the venom gland.
